summary: Defines an optional Content-MD5 header field, a message integrity check that lets the receiver verify the decoded data is the same data that was sent. It was replaced by RFC 1864.

eli5.summary: You put a short fingerprint of a package on the outside. The receiver checks it, and if the fingerprint does not match, something changed.

questions: how to verify email message integrity
subtitle: A message integrity check for MIME mail.

tldr.problem: Email messages can be damaged or altered during transport, and receivers need a way to verify that decoded data is intact.
tldr.mechanism: The sender computes an MD5 checksum of the original data, encodes it in base64, and adds it as an optional Content-MD5 header field. The receiver recomputes the checksum after decoding and compares it.
tldr.outcome: The receiver can detect accidental corruption, but this protects only against accidents, not deliberate tampering. It was replaced by RFC 1864 for clarifications and later superseded by signed/encrypted mail approaches.

today: RFC 1544 defines the Content-MD5 header field as an Internet Standard. It was replaced by RFC 1864 for clarifications, and later systems use cryptographic signing or encryption for stronger integrity and authenticity guarantees.

sections.title: The Problem and Solution
sections.content:
MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) provides tools to encode and protect message data, but accidents can still happen in transit. The Content-MD5 header is an optional integrity check: the sender computes an MD5 message digest of the decoded data before encoding, and the receiver verifies it matches after decoding.

MD5 is a 128-bit hash algorithm that produces a short fingerprint of data; any change to the data changes the fingerprint with high probability. Only the originating user agent should generate this field, never a message relay or gateway.
sections.eli5: The sender takes a fingerprint of the real data. The receiver decodes and fingerprints it too. If the fingerprints match, nothing got scrambled.

sections.title: Computing and Sending the Field
sections.content:
To generate Content-MD5, the sender applies the MD5 algorithm to the raw, canonicalized data—before any content-transfer-encoding like base64. For text, canonical form means each newline is a CR-LF pair. The resulting 128-bit digest becomes 16 bytes, which are encoded in base64 to produce an ASCII header value.

The field can only be used with leaf MIME entities (any content type except multipart or message/rfc822). It is recommended whenever integrity is desired but Privacy-Enhanced Mail is not available. Content-transfer-encoding should be quoted-printable or base64 to avoid trailing-whitespace corruption.
sections.eli5: The sender fingerprints the original data, converts it to text, and puts it in the header. The receiver decodes, fingerprints again, and checks if they match.

sections.title: Receiving and Verifying
sections.content:
A recipient can use the Content-MD5 field to verify that a MIME entity has not been modified during transport. The receiver undoes any content-transfer-encoding, recomputes the MD5 digest, and compares it to the field value. Message gateways must not alter their processing based on this field and may only remove it if the entity's content type changes.

This mechanism detects accidental changes, such as corruption or whitespace loss, but does not protect against deliberate tampering or forgery. For stronger security, Privacy-Enhanced Mail or later encrypted/signed mail systems are recommended.
sections.eli5: The receiver decodes the message, makes its own fingerprint, and compares it to the header. If they match, the message got through unchanged.
